name: Charoite
physical: Traditionally associated with relaxation and restful sleep
Crystal healers link it with easing tension headaches
Often kept nearby during stressful times
summary: Charoite is a swirling lavender-to-violet stone found only in Siberia, known as the stone of transformation, compassion and releasing fear.
intro: Charoite is one of the world's most distinctive gem stones: a swirling, fibrous mass of lavender, violet and deep purple, often threaded with black aegirine, grey feldspar and orange tinges. When cut across the grain, the silky fibres produce a chatoyant sheen, like moiré silk. It occurs in a single area of Siberia, near the Chara River, which makes every piece a rarity by geography alone. It polishes to a glossy finish, and is used for cabochons, spheres, beads, carvings and decorative objects. A good piece looks like a purple galaxy caught in stone.
history: Charoite was known to local people in the Murun Massif for generations, but it only came to the attention of the outside world in the 1940s when Russian geologists described it. It was named after the Chara River in the Sakha Republic of Siberia, though some also suggest the Russian word for charm or magic. It was officially recognised as a new mineral in 1978 and entered the gem trade in the 1970s and 1980s. Because it forms only in one place, its supply has always been limited, which has made it a collector's prize and a symbol of Siberian mineral wealth.
meaning: Charoite is known as the stone of transformation. Practitioners link it with the crown, third eye and heart, using it to ease fear of change and encourage a compassionate view of others and of yourself. Its swirling pattern is seen as a symbol of the twists and turns of a life path, with the purple pointing toward spiritual growth. People use it when they feel overwhelmed or stuck, believing it brings a sense of acceptance and a willingness to let go of old patterns. It is also associated with intuition and vivid dreaming, and is often used by those exploring spiritual practices. Many describe it as a calming but powerful stone.
howToUse: Hold a polished piece during meditation, letting your eyes follow the swirls and your breath slow down. Place it on your brow or crown while lying down for a short rest. Keep a tumble on your bedside table for reflection or dream journaling. Wear it as a pendant to carry a reminder of change as growth. In grids, set it at the centre with amethyst and clear quartz to create a transformation layout. It is also lovely as a display sphere in a quiet corner of a room.
care: Charoite is moderately hard, with a fibrous structure that can chip, so handle it with care. A short rinse in lukewarm water is generally safe, but avoid soaking, ultrasonic cleaners and harsh chemicals, and dry it afterward. Cleanse by smoke, sound or selenite, and charge under the moon. Prolonged sunlight may fade the colour, so avoid long direct sun. Store separately in a soft pouch away from harder stones to protect the polish and prevent scratching.
identify: Genuine charoite shows swirling, fibrous patterns in purple with silky, chatoyant sheen, often with black aegirine and white or grey feldspar. It is only found in Siberia, so claims of other origins are suspicious. Common fakes include dyed howlite, dyed quartzite, purple-dyed marble and resin composites. Look for natural irregularity in the patterns and a silky shimmer that moves as the stone turns. Uniform, pale or perfectly even purple suggests dye or reconstituted stone.

faq.a: In crystal tradition, charoite is a stone of transformation, acceptance and compassion, linked with the crown, third eye and heart. It is used in meditation. These are metaphysical beliefs, not medical claims.
Gem charoite comes from just one place in the world, the Murun Massif near the Chara River in Siberia, Russia. This single source is why it is considered rare and why the supply is limited.
A brief rinse in lukewarm water is generally fine, but avoid long soaks and strong chemicals. Dry it well. Many people prefer smoke, sound or selenite to protect the polish.
